name: Offline password cracking (§3)
description: Feed recovered hash material (kerberoast and AS-REP tickets, NTLM/NTDS dumps, captured NetNTLMv2, /etc/shadow entries) to hashcat or john and recover the plaintext. It all runs offline on your own box and touches no target, so these steps auto-advance; a cracked hash stays a candidate secret until a real login proves it.

actions.title: Identify an Unknown Hash
actions.hypothesis: Pinning down the hash format before cracking keeps you from burning hours on the wrong hashcat mode.
actions.proves: the likely hash type and cracker mode to use (hashcat --identify records hash.type{mode})
actions.does_not_prove: anything about the plaintext behind it

actions.title: Hashcat/John Won't Load the Hash — Fix It
actions.hypothesis: 'No hashes loaded' or 'Token length exception' is not a tough hash - the file or mode is wrong. The usual culprits: a username: prefix left on the line (or missing when the mode wants it), the wrong -m mode for the hash type, CRLF line endings from a Windows copy, or stray whitespace. Fix the file and it cracks.
actions.proves: nothing attack-wise; it gets the cracker to actually load and run on your hash
actions.does_not_prove: that the password is in your wordlist — that is a separate question

commands.note: Identify the type and the exact hashcat -m / john --format. 'Token length exception' almost always means the -m mode does not match the hash you pasted.

commands.run: hashcat -m {{mode}} hash.txt {{wordlist}}   # strip/keep the user: prefix to match the mode
commands.note: NetNTLMv2/Kerberos modes WANT user$realm in the line; raw-MD5/NTLM modes do NOT — 'No hashes loaded' is usually a prefix mismatch. Also run `dos2unix hash.txt` and remove trailing spaces.
The john equivalent: pick the matching --format. 'No password hashes loaded' means the format is wrong or the line is malformed.
GPU/OPENCL ERROR (common in a VM): 'No devices found/left' means no usable GPU. --force runs anyway and -D 1 uses the CPU. Slower, but it cracks; or crack on the host, not the VM.

actions.title: Crack a Kerberoast (TGS) Hash
actions.hypothesis: Service accounts frequently use weak, human-chosen passwords, so a cracked $krb5tgs$ ticket hands you the service account's plaintext.
actions.proves: the plaintext password recovered from a kerberoast hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack an AS-REP Roast Hash
actions.hypothesis: An account without Kerberos pre-auth is AS-REP-roastable: the $krb5asrep$ hash it yields cracks to that user's plaintext.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from an AS-REP hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a Dumped NTLM Hash
actions.hypothesis: An NTLM hash pulled from SAM or NTDS may crack to a plaintext that logs in here or is reused elsewhere.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from an NTLM hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a login on its own, and note the NT hash is already usable for pass-the-hash without any cracking

actions.title: Crack a Captured NetNTLMv2 Hash
actions.hypothesis: A NetNTLMv2 hash captured by Responder or a relay cracks to the account's plaintext; unlike an NT hash it cannot be passed, so cracking is the only route.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a NetNTLMv2 capture
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a Linux /etc/shadow Hash
actions.hypothesis: A shadow entry you can read (via a SUID binary, a backup, or a misconfig) cracks to a local password that is often reused for sudo.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a shadow hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a login or sudo right until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a Password-Protected Archive (zip/rar/7z)
actions.hypothesis: A password-protected backup/export archive found in loot usually hides config files or credentials. Extract its hash with the matching *2john and crack it offline; then unpack it on your box and paste anything credential-like from inside back on Evidence.
actions.proves: the archive password (a candidate secret until it unlocks the archive and its contents are read back)
actions.does_not_prove: any access, the password only unlocks the file; what's inside must still be extracted and validated

commands.note: for a .zip, use the archive obol flagged as loot.material
for a .rar
for a .7z (needs the john-jumbo build)
john auto-detects the *2john format; unzip with the cracked password, then paste any creds/config from inside on Evidence.

actions.title: Online Password Brute over SSH (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: When SSH is reachable once you hold an enumerated user list, a targeted hydra run against an enumerated user list can recover a login, a noisy, lockout-risky attack, so it is approve-tier and never auto-fires in a normal cruise.
actions.proves: a working SSH login (hydra's success line parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra actually returns a hit

commands.note: Fills from your enumerated user list ({{userlist}}); this move only appears once you have one. -f stops on first hit. Mind lockout policy (policy.lockout).

actions.title: Blind SSH Brute (Common Users, Last Resort)
actions.hypothesis: When SSH is open, you have NO enumerated user list, and nothing else is panning out, a blind hydra run against a SHORT common-users wordlist (root, admin, common service names) plus a common-password list can occasionally catch a default or weak login. It is a true last resort: slow, noisy, and lockout-prone, so it sits at the bottom and never leads.
actions.proves: a working SSH login if hydra returns a hit against a common account
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra actually returns a hit; a clean run just means common creds did not work

commands.note: Short COMMON-users list, not an enumerated one. If a login lands, stop and pivot. Do not grind rockyou blindly or you will lock accounts; this is the move of last resort.

actions.title: Online Password Brute over FTP (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: A reachable FTP service with no known credential is a classic hydra target; a recovered login often reuses onto other services.
actions.proves: a working FTP login (parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra returns a hit

commands.note: Fills from your enumerated user list ({{userlist}}); this move only appears once you have one. -f stops on first hit. Mind lockout policy (policy.lockout).

actions.title: Online Password Brute over RDP (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: A reachable RDP service with no known credential can be sprayed with hydra; go slow to avoid account lockout.
actions.proves: a working RDP login (parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra returns a hit

commands.note: Fills from your enumerated user list ({{userlist}}); this move only appears once you have one. -f stops on first hit. Mind lockout policy (policy.lockout).

actions.title: Crack an MS Cache v2 (DCC2) Hash
actions.hypothesis: Domain Cached Credentials v2 ($DCC2$) are stored on a workstation so a domain user can log in offline. They are deliberately slow to crack, but a weak password still falls, and the plaintext is a real domain credential to reuse. Pulled from a local secretsdump (the cachedump).
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a cached domain credential (DCC2)
actions.does_not_prove: a fast result, DCC2 is intentionally slow; and the hash cannot be passed (unlike NTLM), so cracking is the only use

commands.note: Mode 2100 = DCC2 / MS-Cache v2.

actions.title: VNC Stored Password Decryption
actions.hypothesis: VNC implementations (TightVNC, UltraVNC, RealVNC) store passwords encrypted with a standardized DES key fixed in the RFB specification. Extracted password registry values or .ini file hex strings can be instantly decrypted offline to plaintext without dictionary cracking.
actions.proves: decrypts cleartext VNC administrative passwords from stored registry keys or configuration files
actions.does_not_prove: access until validated against open VNC (port 5900) or reused against SSH/WinRM/SMB

report.finding: Insecure VNC Password Storage (Reversible RFB Encryption)

commands.note: PREFERRED: Built-in Kali/Linux tool to decrypt VNC hex strings or TightVNC .reg exports into plaintext.
Python standalone RFB DES decryptor for raw hex strings found in configs or memory dumps.

actions.title: KeePass Memory Dump Recovery (CVE-2023-32784) & Hash Cracking
actions.hypothesis: KeePass 2.x versions prior to 2.54 leave cleartext password characters in process memory during entry editing (CVE-2023-32784). If a process memory dump (.dmp or crash dump) is discovered, specialized parsers can reconstruct the KeePass master password. If an encrypted database (.kdbx) is obtained, keepass2john extracts the crackable hash for offline password recovery.
actions.proves: recovers candidate master passwords from KeePass process dumps or extracts crackable master password hashes from KDBX databases
actions.does_not_prove: does not prove database unlock until the candidate master password successfully decrypts the KDBX file

report.finding: KeePass Master Password Recoverable from Memory Dump (CVE-2023-32784)

commands.note: PREFERRED (Memory Dump Master Key Recovery): Reconstructs master password character candidates from KeePass process dump memory (CVE-2023-32784).
OFFLINE KDBX HASH CRACKING: Extracts the master key hash from an encrypted KeePass database file and cracks with John the Ripper.

commands.run: python3 -c "import pykeepass; kp = pykeepass.PyKeePass('{{kdbx_file}}', password='{{password}}'); [print(e.title, e.username, e.password) for e in kp.entries]"
commands.note: DECRYPT KDBX ENTRIES: With the recovered master password, unlock the KDBX database and print all stored usernames, passwords, and URLs.

actions.title: Cisco Password Decryption and Hash Cracking
actions.hypothesis: Cisco configuration files frequently contain obfuscated Type 7 passwords or salted Type 5/8/9 hashes. Type 7 uses a reversible Vigenère cipher instantly decrypted with cisco-decrypt. Type 5 (md5crypt) and Type 8/9 (PBKDF2/scrypt) are cracked offline with Hashcat (-m 500 / -m 9200 / -m 9300) or John the Ripper.
actions.proves: decrypted cleartext or cracked Cisco administrative passwords
actions.does_not_prove: network device or host access until authenticated against a live service

report.finding: Cisco Obfuscated or Weak Password Recovered

commands.note: Reversibly decrypts Cisco Type 7 passwords (e.g. password 7 0822455B10D00F1654).
Cracks Cisco Type 5 MD5-crypt hashes (enable secret 5 $1$...) using wordlists.
John the Ripper alternative for Cisco Type 5 secret cracking.
